shorts_extract.hook: In 1999 at Harvard, volunteers counted basketball passes between players in white shirts while a person in a full gorilla suit walked into the middle of the game, faced the camera, and thumped her chest for nine seconds—and half of all viewers never saw the gorilla.
shorts_extract.core_experiment: Simons and Chabris filmed three White-team players and three Black-team players weaving in front of three elevator doors in William James Hall; focusing hard on counting white-shirt passes caused the parietal cortex attention spotlight to suppress the dark gorilla even after its image reached the primary visual cortex.
shorts_extract.twist: Eye-tracking proved that people who missed the gorilla stared directly at it for one full second, and when researchers hid a gorilla inside lung CT scans, 83% of expert radiologists looked right at it and missed it too.

chapters.title: The 1999 Harvard Elevator Lobby Test
beats: Cold open on the 14th-floor elevator landing of William James Hall: three steel elevator doors, six students in white and black t-shirts, two bouncing orange basketballs.
The viewer challenge: count the White team's 15 passes as the gorilla walks into the center, faces the camera, thumps her chest for 9 seconds, and exits.
The reveal: 50% of viewers in the chest-thumping condition (and 46% across all 192 observers in the 16 main conditions) miss the gorilla completely.

chapters.title: From Ulric Neisser's Umbrella Woman to Jerome Kagan's Gorilla Suit
beats: Why scientists doubted earlier blindness studies: Ulric Neisser's 1975–1979 half-silvered mirror umbrella woman and Arien Mack & Irvin Rock's 1998 200-ms computer cross flashes.
How Daniel Simons and Christopher Chabris borrowed developmental psychologist Jerome Kagan's gorilla costume and recruited student Elisa Cheng to test live-action occlusion.

chapters.title: Why Counting White Shirts Erases a Black Gorilla
beats: The 2x2x2x2 experimental breakdown: Easy total pass count (64% noticed) vs Hard bounce-and-aerial count (45% noticed).
The feature-similarity discovery: 58% of Black-team trackers noticed the black gorilla, but only 27% of White-team trackers noticed it (73% missed it).
Inside the brain: raw light from the gorilla hits the primary visual cortex (vision center), but the parietal cortex (attention spotlight) suppresses dark shapes while boosting white shirts.

chapters.title: Staring Straight Through the Gorilla: Eye-Tracking & Brain Scans
beats: Debunking the 'looking away' excuse: Daniel Memmert's 2006 eye-tracking study proving non-noticers fixated directly on the gorilla for ~1 full second.
Debunking 'inattentional amnesia' (Rees et al. 1999 Science fMRI study) and the 'smart/high-working-memory people don't miss it' myth (Bredemeier & Simons 2012).

chapters.title: When Experts Miss the Gorilla: Radiologists & Police Chases
beats: Drew, Võ & Wolfe (2013): 20 out of 24 (83%) expert radiologists miss a gorilla 48 times the size of a cancer nodule in chest CT scans despite looking straight at it.
Chabris et al. (2011) 'Fight Club' replication of the Boston police officer Kenny Conley case: runners chasing a suspect miss a loud 3-man brawl right beside the path.
Simons (2010) 'The Monkey Business Illusion': viewers hunting for the gorilla miss the red curtain turning gold and a player leaving the game.

chapters.title: The Illusion of Attention in Everyday Life
beats: How inattentional blindness causes 'looked-but-failed-to-see' car crashes against cyclists and motorcycles (Strayer et al. 2003) and cell-phone walking blindness (Hyman et al. 2010).
Practical takeaway: why lowering cognitive load and knowing your attention spotlight is narrow is the only defense against missing what stands right in front of you.
